concepts.def: An optical component, usually of glass or plastic, that forms an image by refracting light. The light is refracted as it enters the lens and again as it leaves, and this change of direction is what brings the rays together or spreads them apart.

A lens that is thicker in the middle than at its edges. Parallel rays of light passing through a convex lens are brought to a focus at the principal focus, so a convex lens is also called a converging lens.

The point at which parallel rays of light are brought to a focus by a convex lens. For a concave lens, parallel rays are spread out so that they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side of the lens as the incoming light.

The distance from the lens to the principal focus. A more powerful lens, which bends light more strongly, has a shorter focal length. The focal length is a property of the lens itself and does not change when the object is moved.

The straight line drawn through the centre of the lens at right angles to it. Ray diagrams are set out along the principal axis, with the principal focus marked on it at the focal length from the lens on each side.
A lens that is thinner in the middle than at its edges. It spreads parallel rays of light apart, so it is also called a diverging lens, and the image it produces is always virtual.

A scale drawing that uses at least two rays from a point on the object to show where the image is formed, how big it is and which way up it is. Ray diagrams are used to show the formation of images by convex and concave lenses.

An image formed where rays of light actually meet after passing through the lens. Because the light really is there, a real image can be projected onto a screen. A real image formed by a convex lens is inverted.

An image formed where rays of light only appear to come from, once they are traced back behind the lens. No light actually meets there, so a virtual image cannot be projected onto a screen, although it can be seen by looking through the lens. A virtual image formed by a lens is upright.

concepts.term: Image produced by a convex lens
concepts.def: It can be either real or virtual. When the object is further from the lens than the principal focus, the refracted rays meet and a real, inverted image is formed. When the object is nearer to the lens than the principal focus, the rays leave still diverging and a virtual, upright, magnified image is formed on the same side as the object.

concepts.term: Image produced by a concave lens
concepts.def: It is always virtual. The refracted rays always leave the lens diverging, so they never meet; traced back, they appear to come from a point between the lens and the principal focus. The image is upright, smaller than the object and on the same side of the lens as the object.

concepts.term: Constructing a ray diagram for a convex lens
concepts.def: Draw the lens symbol on the principal axis and mark the principal focus at the focal length on each side. From the top of the object draw a ray parallel to the axis, refracted through the principal focus on the far side, and a ray straight through the centre of the lens, which is undeviated. Where these two rays cross is the top of a real image; if they do not cross, trace them back to find the virtual image.

concepts.term: Constructing a ray diagram for a concave lens
concepts.def: Draw the lens symbol on the principal axis and mark the principal focus on each side. From the top of the object draw a ray parallel to the axis, which is refracted so that it appears to come from the principal focus on the same side as the object, and a ray straight through the centre of the lens, which is undeviated. Trace the refracted rays back until they meet to locate the virtual image.

Both form images by refracting light, both are drawn on a principal axis with a principal focus at the focal length, and in both the ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on. They differ in what they do to parallel rays: the convex lens brings them to a focus, while the concave lens spreads them apart. Because of this the convex lens can produce a real or a virtual image, whereas the concave lens always produces a virtual one.

The magnification produced by a lens can be calculated using the equation: magnification = (image height)/(object height). This equation is supplied on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so the skill assessed is selecting it and applying it correctly rather than recalling it. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; a magnification less than 1 means it is smaller.

Magnification is a ratio — a height divided by a height — so the units cancel and the answer is a plain number with no unit after it. Writing '3 cm' or '3 mm' for a magnification is wrong; the answer is simply 3.

concepts.term: Measuring image height and object height
concepts.def: Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm. What matters is that the same unit is used for both, because the ratio is only correct when the two heights are expressed in the same unit; if one is given in mm and the other in cm, convert one of them first.

In ray diagrams a convex lens is represented by a vertical straight line drawn across the principal axis with an arrowhead at each end, both pointing outwards, away from the axis. The outward arrowheads are a reminder that the lens is thicker in the middle.

A concave lens is represented by a vertical straight line drawn across the principal axis with an arrowhead at each end, both pointing inwards, towards the axis. The inward arrowheads are a reminder that the lens is thinner in the middle.

mcqs.q: A beam of rays travelling parallel to the principal axis passes through a convex lens. What happens to the rays?
options: They are reflected from the lens surface to a point in front
They are refracted so that they meet at the principal focus
They are refracted so that they meet at the focal length
They carry straight on, since they strike the lens head-on
mcqs.explain: This is the definition given in the specification: in a convex lens, parallel rays of light are brought to a focus at the principal focus.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the focal length of a convex lens?
options: The distance from the lens to the image it produces
The distance the object must be to give a sharp image
The distance from the lens to the principal focus
The length of the lens across its widest part
mcqs.explain: This is exactly how the specification defines the focal length.

mcqs.q: A lens forms an image. Where is the light changed in direction?
options: It is reflected from both surfaces of the lens
It is refracted only at the surface where it leaves
It is diffracted as it spreads out inside the glass
It is refracted as it enters and as it leaves the lens
mcqs.explain: A lens forms an image by refracting light, and refraction occurs at each boundary the light crosses.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the image produced by a concave lens is correct?
options: It is real when the object is beyond the principal focus
It is real and inverted, like a convex lens image
It is virtual only when the object is close to the lens
It is always virtual, whatever the object distance
mcqs.explain: The specification states without exception that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.

mcqs.q: An object is placed between a convex lens and its principal focus. What kind of image is formed?
options: A real image, inverted and larger than the object
A virtual image, upright and larger than the object
A virtual image, upright and smaller than the object
A real image, inverted and smaller than the object
mcqs.explain: The refracted rays leave still diverging, so they never meet; traced back they give an upright, magnified virtual image. This is the magnifying glass.

mcqs.q: Which observation shows that an image formed by a lens is real rather than virtual?
options: It can be seen by an eye that looks through the lens
It is the same way up as the object that produced it
It is smaller than the object that produced it
It can be formed on a screen placed where the rays meet
mcqs.explain: A real image is formed where light rays actually meet, so light really arrives at the screen and a picture appears on it.

mcqs.q: In a ray diagram for a convex lens, how is the ray from the top of the object to the centre of the lens drawn?
options: It is refracted towards the principal focus
It is refracted so that it leaves parallel to the axis
It carries straight on without changing direction
It is reflected back along the path it came
mcqs.explain: At the centre the two surfaces are parallel, so the ray emerges in its original direction; this straight ray fixes the image position.

mcqs.q: In a ray diagram for a concave lens, a ray arrives parallel to the principal axis. How is it drawn after the lens?
options: It converges to the principal focus beyond the lens
It carries straight on, since the lens cannot focus it
It diverges, as if it had come from the principal focus
It travels back towards the object along the same path
mcqs.explain: A concave lens spreads light apart; traced backwards the refracted ray passes through the principal focus on the object side, which is why the image is virtual.

mcqs.q: A student draws ray diagrams for a convex lens and a concave lens using the same object. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both refract the light, but only the convex lens converges it
Both refract the light, and both can produce a real image
Only the convex lens refracts light, the concave one reflects
Both produce virtual images, but the convex one is inverted
mcqs.explain: The similarity is the mechanism — both form images by refraction — and the difference is that the convex lens brings parallel rays to a focus while the concave lens spreads them.

mcqs.q: An object 5 mm tall produces an image 15 mm tall. What is the magnification?
options: 3 mm
mcqs.explain: magnification = image height / object height = 15 mm / 5 mm = 3.

mcqs.q: An object 8.0 cm tall produces an image 2.4 cm tall. What is the magnification?
options: 0.3 cm
mcqs.explain: magnification = image height / object height = 2.4 cm / 8.0 cm = 0.3, a number below 1 because the image is smaller.

mcqs.q: An object 40 mm tall produces an image 8.0 cm tall. What is the magnification?
mcqs.explain: Convert first: 8.0 cm = 80 mm, so magnification = 80 mm / 40 mm = 2.

mcqs.q: How should the magnification produced by a lens be written?
options: As a number on its own, since it is a ratio
In centimetres, since heights are given in cm
In millimetres, since the ruler reads in mm
As a number greater than 1, since images grow
mcqs.explain: Magnification is a ratio and so has no units: a height divided by a height leaves a pure number.

mcqs.q: In ray diagrams, which symbol is used to represent a convex lens?
options: A vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards
A vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing outwards
A vertical line with a single arrowhead at its upper end only
A curved line that bulges outwards on both of its two faces
mcqs.explain: This is the symbol the specification gives for a convex lens; the outward arrowheads match a lens that is thicker in the middle.

mcqs.q: A ray diagram shows a vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards. Which lens is this, and what does it do to parallel rays?
options: A concave lens, which spreads parallel rays apart
A convex lens, which brings parallel rays to a focus
A convex lens, which spreads parallel rays apart
A concave lens, which brings parallel rays to a focus
mcqs.explain: Inward arrowheads represent the concave lens, which is thinner in the middle and diverges parallel rays.
